title: The Paradox of Telling People You’re Competent
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author identifies a paradox in self-description: people who announce that they are competent, humble or empathetic make listeners doubt exactly that quality. Genuine strength is demonstrated through work rather than declared, and the same logic extends to nearly every virtue. The post is careful to say that promoting accomplishments is acceptable and even expected, because track records tell others what to anticipate. The problem lies narrowly in applying a virtue label to oneself, which reads as grandiose and self-contradictory. The same applies to calling oneself successful, where describing the success or saying lucky or fortunate lands better.
points: Self-applied virtue labels trigger suspicion because they invite the question of why the evidence is not speaking for itself.
The line the author draws is between describing outcomes and track record, which is fine, and labeling oneself with a virtue, which is not.
The principle covers integrity, humility, empathy and wisdom, not only competence.
Words like lucky, fortunate or blessed are presented as more likable substitutes for calling oneself successful.
quotes: People are suspicious of anyone who labels themselves as competent. The thinking goes that those who have to broadcast that they have significant strengths and proficiencies must lack capability. Only an unskillful leader would find the need to tell others about their competencies.
Those confident in their skills prefer to let their work speak for itself. This is the age-old idea that actions speak more loudly than words.
Those with integrity don’t have to tell others how honest they are. Leaders with humility don’t describe themselves as humble. Leaders with true empathy don’t describe themselves as empathetic.

This is not to say that good leaders never promote their work or profile their milestones and successes. Encouraging others to learn about what we are capable of by describing our outcomes or track record is both expected and rewarded.

It is primarily the self-reference that creates the paradox. Referring to yourself as possessing any virtue sets off alarm bells. Why would you need to do that unless you couldn’t show others that virtue through your actions or offer evidence that confirms the internal strength exists?

The lesson here is to avoid referring to yourself in grandiose terms. Labeling yourself as competent or humble or nearly any other virtuous designation is seen as both grandiose and self-contradictory.
